subtype: Approach: asking for a job in the first message [Pitfall]
passage:
The referral window at the logistics company closed on Friday, and Baljeet had only found out on Wednesday night. Her college had no alumni there. Scrolling a professional networking site on a crowded bus, she found Urmila, a senior analyst at the company, with a clear profile photo and a long list of projects.
Baljeet typed with one thumb: 'Hello ma'am, I am a final-year student. Please refer me for the analyst role. My resume is attached. Thank you.'
She sent it before the bus reached her stop.
Thursday: no reply. Friday: the message still showed as unread. The window closed at midnight.
On Saturday Baljeet reread her message and felt her face go hot. There was nothing in it about Urmila, nothing about why Baljeet wanted that team, nothing that gave a stranger a reason to put her own name next to Baljeet's.

qa.q: When did the referral window close?
qa.a: It closed on Friday at midnight.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling on Saturday when she reread the message?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, her face going hot, as she saw the message gave a stranger no reason to vouch for her.

qa.q: What would you change first about Baljeet's message?
qa.a: Open with something specific about Urmila's work and ask one small question or a short call first, before any request for a referral.

qa.q: How might the message look to Urmila, if she had opened it?
qa.a: To Urmila it would read as a stranger asking her to risk her own name, with no context or connection to justify it.

grounding: Shows a student asking a stranger for a referral in the very first message, which goes unanswered because nothing builds context or trust.

subtype: Approach: asking for a job in the first message [Pitfall]
passage:
In a Pune café near her college, Jyoti opened the profile of Madhuri Kulkarni, a hiring manager at a payments firm she badly wanted to join, and typed fast: 'Hi, I'm looking for a job in your company. Can you refer me? I can send my CV.'
She sent the same text to four more people at the firm that evening.
A week later, not one had replied. On a call with her friend Keshav, Jyoti grumbled that people who got in never helped anyone else. 'They're so arrogant,' she said, and shut her laptop hard.
Keshav asked her to paste the message. After reading it, he said slowly, 'She doesn't know you. You asked for the biggest favour in the first line.'
Jyoti read it again. Then she opened Madhuri's profile and, for the first time, read what Madhuri had written about her team's work.

qa.q: How many more people at the firm got the same text?
qa.a: Four more people at the firm.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she shut the laptop hard?
qa.a: She felt angry and rejected, blaming the people who got in instead of looking at her own message.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Jyoti better now?
qa.a: Learn about Madhuri's team first and write a short note with a specific question, building some connection before any mention of a referral.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see a message like that from a stranger?
qa.a: Madhuri would likely see a request with no context or relationship, and would have no reason to put her name behind it.

grounding: Shows a student asking strangers for a referral in the first message, getting no replies, and blaming them until a friend points out the missing context.
